A Tear-Stained Celebration of Overflowing Love, Mexican Heritage, and the Power of Memory.180303 (5.0)Cheeks soaked in tears, brimming with an overwhelming pour of love. The traditions of Día de los Muertos and Mexican music are melted together so brilliantly. Directed by Lee Unkrich and co-directed by Adrian Molina, the 2017 Pixar animated feature "Coco" follows 12-year-old Miguel, an aspiring musician who finds himself accidentally transported to the vibrant Land of the Dead despite his family's generations-old ban on music. Teaming up with the charming trickster Héctor to uncover the real story behind his musical heritage, the film delivers a visually dazzling and deeply resonant journey that honors ancestral remembrance, family bonds, and the unforgettable power of song to bridge the living and the departed.

Pixar explores Mexican culture, probing the spirituality and mythos of Day of the Dead while digging into a family conflict that's several generations old.

It's a visual, audible and emotional delight, enlivened with loud splashes of color and texture, and accompanied by a constantly upbeat musical vitality. There's no escaping the visual fabric of this film, immersive and jaw-dropping, as it constantly one-ups itself right alongside the developing plot. Particularly stunning is our crossing into the land of the deceased, a monumental city of stacked shanties that shimmers and glistens and pulses as its residents decorate and celebrate their annual recognition.

The story is simple but effective, perhaps a touch on the predictable side... but so are many animated classics, and sometimes there's something to be said for following through on a promise. Coco wears its heart on its sleeve, with a permeating, spirited warmth that's impossible to ignore, while also touching on tricky, lingering feelings of betrayal and repression.

Dazzling and optimistic, with a subject that's, surprisingly, never been explored with such playful reverence in a major family film. Good to see the studio has kept tabs on that bottled magic; for a while, I worried they'd misplaced it.

"Coco." Released in 2017, this animated gem takes us on a musical journey through Mexican culture and the afterlife. So, let's strum the chords of emotion and dissect what makes "Coco" hit all the right notes.

Visual Aesthetics:
First off, let's talk visuals. "Coco" is a feast for the eyes, a kaleidoscope of colors and meticulously crafted animation. Pixar once again proves its mastery in creating immersive worlds, and the Land of the Dead is a breathtaking spectacle. The attention to detail, from the marigold petals to the intricacies of the skeletal characters, is nothing short of awe-inspiring. It's a visual fiesta that celebrates the richness of Mexican folklore and tradition.

Soundtrack:
Now, the soundtrack. Oh, mama, the music in "Coco" is like a soul-stirring serenade. The original songs, composed by Michael Giacchino and Kristen Anderson-Lopez, capture the essence of Mexican music with infectious energy. The standout track, "Remember Me," is an emotional powerhouse that tugs at the heartstrings. It's a soundtrack that not only complements the narrative but elevates it to another level, making you want to dance, cry, and celebrate life all at once

Story and Characters:
Let's dive into the narrative and characters. "Coco" follows the journey of Miguel, a young boy with dreams of becoming a musician, as he ventures into the Land of the Dead. The film weaves a poignant tale about family, legacy, and the importance of remembering those who came before us. The characters are richly developed, and the familial dynamics resonate on a universal level. Miguel's journey is both personal and universal, making it a narrative that transcends cultural boundaries.

Themes:
Now, let's talk themes. "Coco" delves into themes of memory, identity, and the power of familial bonds. It explores the idea that our ancestors live on through the memories we keep and the stories we tell. The film does this with a delicate touch, avoiding heavy-handed sentimentality and instead delivering a message that feels genuine and profound.

In the grand Pixar tapestry, "Coco" is a standout thread, a film that not only entertains but educates and resonates on a deeply emotional level. It's a celebration of Mexican culture that doesn't resort to clichés or stereotypes but embraces the beauty of tradition and the importance of remembering our roots.

It's a masterpiece of animation, storytelling, and cultural representation.

I went to see this movie in theatres with my grandfather and walked out completely stunned by what I'd seen. I expected 'Coco' to be a Mexican 'Moana' (I was 12 back then, so Disney and Pixar were all same to me), but got something way better. This is one of Pixar's most memorable films- the songs, the worldbuilding, and of course, who can forget the humor, which is unpredictable beyond imagination. A double emotional climax, like the one we got in 'Toy Story 3' is all fine, but where this film excels is in empathy. To me, Pixar stories are all about accepting people for who they are, and this movie goes even further. That's reflected in the fact that this movie celebrates a culture foreign to America. There's a Ghibli movie called 'Grave of the fireflies' that can make a big brother care more for his little sister. 'Coco' is a movie that does the same for one's family. A must-see for all ages, and as a family if possible.

I loved this film, primarily for the mix of high quality music (latin) and the immersive, CGI animation. The themes are nice and I suppose very young children may struggle a little to follow all the messages - it could be mildly scary for very young kids but then it does have a PG rating, so that's fair. Its a nice, uplifting and cheery film, even though it very much focuses on the dead - indeed its set during 'la dia de las muerteas', aka 'The Day of the Dead' which is celebrated in Mexico. If you enjoy Pixar films, then I would recommend this film, in terms of the overall feel it gives out - its a bit of a warm hug of a film, as I say re-assuring, nice and not expressly too cinnamon sweet in a bad way. However, if you can't stand CGI animation, then obviously this won't be for you. I also enjoyed the variety of characters, with a rather zany stray/street dog called Dante being one and I also wondered if the inspiration behind the more villainous characters, had been taken from a telenovela (aka latin American soaps).

This isn't entirely a dumbed-down film and I would highly recommend it for family viewing overall, yes. Oh, and if you enjoy the guitar music, you might want to watch (or shall I say, listen) through the credits while it keeps playing. Its quite soothing and enjoyable.

I love this movie.  Coco is easily PIXAR's best movie since Inside Out, it's not even close.  Coco is a delight from start to finish.  The characters are really really good, which is a compliment I haven't given to many recent PIXAR flicks.  The music is also outstanding.  The animation syncs so well with all the music especially when characters play guitar; the animation is once again extremely impressive, which has become a cliche to say.  I always cry at the end of this movie, it moves me every time.  This movie is also a great dive into Mexican culture, which was really cool to see.  The skeletons look fantastic.  The Land of the Dead is gorgeous and a really cool world to see.  Coming right after Cars 3, this movie is a huge breath of fresh air.  From here on out, I really enjoy the rest of PIXAR's movies (as of early 2021), and it started with Coco, which I consider to be the start of a PIXAR renaissance.
